How to calculate net proceeds from selling a house

Net proceeds are the money left after everything the sale costs and after your mortgage is paid off. Take the sale price, subtract each cost, and what remains is the cash you receive at closing. Here is a $450,000 sale worked line by line. Cash at closing comes to $206,450.

Open the free calculator

The example sale

Sale price$450,000
Mortgage payoff$212,000
Each agent commission, 2.5%$11,250
Title and escrow, 1%$4,500
Transfer tax, 0.5%$2,250
Other costs$500
Prorated property tax$1,800

Step 1: add up the selling costs

Two commissions of $11,250 are $22,500. Add $4,500 for title and escrow, $2,250 for transfer tax and $500 of other costs: $29,750, which is 6.6% of the price.

Step 2: subtract the payoff and prorations

$450,000 − $29,750 − $212,000 − $1,800 = $206,450 cash at closing.

Step 3: check whether the sale is taxed

Say the home cost $120,000 plus $4,000 of buying costs and $25,000 of improvements, so the basis is $149,000. The amount realized is $450,000 − $29,750 = $420,250, so the gain is $271,250. A single filer who lived there two of the last five years excludes $250,000, leaving $21,250 taxable. With $95,000 of other income and a 4% state rate, the estimated tax is $4,037.50.

Step 4: the net after tax and prep

$206,450 − $3,500 of prep before listing − $4,037.50 of tax = $198,912.50.

Working backwards from a target

Every cost scales with the price, so wanting $250,000 at closing does not mean listing at $250,000 plus the payoff. In this example the sale price has to be about $496,578. The calculator solves for that price. It also compares offers: a higher price with a large concession can leave you with less than a clean lower offer.

Run your own numbers

Common questions

What is a seller net sheet?

A seller net sheet is an estimate of the money you will receive at closing after the sale price is reduced by commissions, closing costs, concessions and your mortgage payoff. This page walks through building one and the calculator does it for you.

How much of the sale price do sellers typically keep?

After commissions and closing costs, sellers typically lose about 6 to 10 percent of the price before their mortgage payoff, so a 450,000 dollar sale usually leaves 405,000 to 423,000 dollars to pay the mortgage and take home.

Does the buyer's agent commission come out of the seller's proceeds?

Usually the seller pays it only if the listing or purchase contract says so. Since 2024 rule changes, buyer agent compensation is negotiated and no longer fixed by the listing, so the calculator has a separate field you can set to zero.

How it is built

Cash at closing: sale price minus both agent commissions, title and escrow, transfer tax, seller concessions, other selling costs, your payoff and prorated taxes. Prep money you spend before listing is subtracted in the after-tax figure.

Tax: gain is the sale price minus selling costs minus your basis (purchase price, buying costs and improvements, less depreciation). The home sale exclusion removes up to 250,000 dollars (500,000 for joint filers), prorated for a partial exclusion. Depreciation is taxed up to 25 percent. Remaining gain is taxed at the 0, 15 or 20 percent long-term rates stacked on top of your other income, plus the 3.8 percent net investment income tax when your income is high enough, plus your state rate. Federal figures are for tax year 2026. A loss on a personal home is not deductible.

List price for a target: net proceeds only ever go up as the price goes up, so the tool searches for the exact price that lands on your target, and the test suite checks that it does across hundreds of random homes.

Common questions

How much will I net from selling my house?

Start with the sale price and subtract agent commissions, title and escrow fees, transfer taxes, any seller concessions, your mortgage payoff and prorated property taxes. What is left is the cash at closing. Then subtract any tax on the gain. Enter your numbers above to see each line.

What price do I need to list at to walk away with a target amount?

Enter the cash you want in the target field and the tool runs the math backwards, because every cost scales with the price. It shows the sale price that leaves you exactly that amount, either as cash at closing or after estimated tax.

Do I owe capital gains tax when I sell my home?

Often not. If you owned and lived in the home for at least two of the last five years, the first 250,000 dollars of gain (500,000 for married couples filing jointly) is excluded from federal tax. Gain above that, and any depreciation you took on a rental or home office, can be taxed. The tool estimates both.

How much does it cost to sell a house?

Typical selling costs run about 6 to 10 percent of the price once commissions, closing fees, transfer taxes, concessions and prep are counted. Your own number depends on your market and contract, so the tool shows your cost of selling as a percentage of the price.

Do home improvements reduce capital gains tax?

Capital improvements such as a new roof, an addition or a remodel add to your tax basis and shrink the gain. Routine repairs and maintenance do not. Enter improvements in the tax section and the tool adjusts the basis.

How do I compare offers with different concessions?

Enter up to three offers with their prices and seller concessions. The tool computes net proceeds for each, so a higher headline price with a large concession can be compared fairly against a lower clean offer.

Is my information uploaded?

No. Everything is calculated in your browser, there are no accounts, and nothing is sent to a server.

Is this tax or financial advice?

No. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, using tax year 2026 federal figures and a flat state rate you provide. Your closing disclosure and a tax professional decide what you actually owe.
